claims.headline: Tabitha Brown turned a 30-day vegan challenge into a lifelong comfort-food philosophy after plant-based eating helped ease her chronic pain
claims.body: Brown has spoken openly about struggling with chronic pain for years before a doctor suggested she try a 30-day vegan challenge in 2017. She documented the experience on social media and found that eating whole plant foods — built around tempeh, jackfruit, black beans, avocado, and generous greens — made her feel better than she had in a long time. Rather than treating veganism as a restrictive health measure, she channeled it into an exuberant comfort-food style that draws on her Southern roots. Her TTLA (tempeh, tomato, lettuce, avocado) sandwich became a viral touchstone for the idea that vegan food can be deeply satisfying, soulful, and simple enough for anyone to make at home. Forks Over Knives profiled her journey as a model for how plant-based eating can be motivating rather than austere.

sources.excerpt: Brown adopted a plant-based diet after a 30-day vegan challenge and found it helped ease the chronic pain she had struggled with for years, going on to share her comfort-food approach with millions.
The actress and social media star credits her vegan lifestyle with helping manage the chronic pain that had plagued her, and has inspired a devoted following with her soulful plant-based recipes.

claims.headline: Brown's cookbook 'Feeding the Soul' frames vegan cooking as an act of self-love rooted in joy, not deprivation
claims.body: In her cookbook Feeding the Soul (Because It's My Business), Brown articulates a food philosophy she describes as cooking from a place of love and abundance. She argues that the biggest barrier to plant-based eating is the mistaken belief that it has to be bland or restrictive. Her recipes are intentionally indulgent in flavor — leaning on smoky spices, creamy avocado, and rich cashew sauces — so that making the vegan choice feels like a reward rather than a sacrifice. People magazine noted that her viral videos work precisely because they broadcast genuine delight, turning every dish into an invitation rather than a lecture.

sources.excerpt: In Feeding the Soul, Brown writes that cooking should come from a place of love and abundance — the antithesis of the deprivation narrative that keeps many people from trying plant-based eating.
